faq.q1: What is compound interest and why does it matter?
faq.q2: How does the SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) calculator work?
faq.q3: What is CAGR and when should I use it?
faq.q4: How should I use the Retirement calculator?
faq.q5: What return rate should I assume in projections?
faq.q6: Are these projections guaranteed? Is this financial advice?
faq.q7: Is my financial data uploaded or stored?
faq.q8: How do compounding frequency choices affect results?
faq.q9: SIP vs lump sum: which grows more?
faq.q11: Can I share or export my calculation?
faq.q12: Who runs this site and how can I reach you?
faq.a1: Compound interest is interest calculated on both your initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods. Unlike simple interest, compounding lets your returns generate their own returns, producing exponential growth over decades — which is why starting early matters so much. Try our Compound Interest Calculator on the homepage to see the curve for yourself.
faq.a2: The SIP calculator projects the future value of fixed monthly investments growing at an assumed annual return. It uses the future value of an annuity: FV = P x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r] x (1 + r), where P is the monthly amount, r the monthly rate and n the number of months. It shows total invested, estimated gains, and a year-by-year chart.
faq.a3: CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) is the smoothed annual rate at which an investment grows from beginning to ending value: CAGR = (Ending / Beginning)^(1 / Years) - 1. Use it to compare investments held over different periods on a like-for-like annual basis. Our CAGR Calculator computes the rate plus total and absolute growth instantly.
faq.a4: Enter your current age, planned retirement age, current savings, monthly contribution and expected annual return. The calculator projects your retirement corpus, total contributions and wealth gained from compounding, with a year-by-year chart. Start with conservative returns (5-7%), then adjust contributions or retirement age to close any gap.
faq.a5: There is no single right number. Test a range: conservative (4-6%), moderate (7-9%) and optimistic (10-12%) for equity-heavy portfolios, lower (2-4%) for savings or bonds. Always run a base case and a conservative case, and subtract expected inflation (often 2-3%) to think in real purchasing-power terms.
faq.a6: No. All outputs are mathematical illustrations based on constant return assumptions. Real markets fluctuate, fees and taxes apply, and actual results will differ. Nothing on this site constitutes financial, investment, tax or legal advice. For personal decisions, consult a licensed professional.
faq.a7: No. All calculations run locally in your browser; we do not receive or store the numbers you type into calculators. Save State encodes configuration into the page URL or browser history, not our servers. Only contact-form messages and newsletter signups are sent to us, covered by the Privacy Policy.
faq.a8: Compounding frequency controls how often earned interest joins the balance. More frequent compounding yields slightly higher results at the same nominal rate — e.g. 8% monthly beats 8% annually. The difference is modest short-term but meaningful over decades, as the calculator demonstrates.
faq.a9: At a constant rate, a lump sum invested on day one always beats the same total dripped in monthly, because more money compounds for longer. In real volatile markets, SIPs reduce timing risk and enforce discipline, which is why most salaried investors prefer them. Use both calculators and compare side by side.
faq.a10: Yes. Use the currency switcher in the header (USD, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY, AUD) and all outputs reformat instantly. The math is currency-agnostic — only the symbol and formatting change.
faq.a11: Yes. Save State encodes your inputs into a shareable URL to bookmark or send to a partner or adviser, and Download PDF exports a summary report with inputs, results and charts for your records.
faq.a12: We are an independent team building free financial-education tools. See the About page for our mission and the Contact page for the support form and email. We welcome feedback, corrections and feature requests, usually replying within 2 business days.

guide.heroTitle: How to Use Our Financial Calculators
guide.metaTitle: User Guide: How to Use Our Financial Calculators
guide.heroDesc: Four tools, one workflow: project growth, set monthly targets, compare past returns fairly, and secure your retirement — in under ten minutes.
guide.s1t: 1. Compound Interest Calculator — model lump-sum growth
guide.s1d: Enter initial investment, monthly contribution (can be 0), expected annual return, horizon in years and compounding frequency. The chart splits your balance between contributions and interest earned. Compare frequencies (monthly vs annually) to feel the compounding effect.
guide.s2d: Enter monthly investment, expected annual return and years. The tool applies FV = P x [((1+r)^n - 1)/r] x (1+r) and shows total invested vs estimated gains. Adjust the amount until the projected value covers your goal.
guide.s3t: 3. CAGR Calculator — compare past performance fairly
guide.s3d: Enter beginning value, ending value and years held. You get CAGR = (End/Start)^(1/Years) - 1 plus total growth. Use it to compare a 3-year stock run against a 7-year fund on equal annualized footing.
guide.s4t: 4. Retirement Calculator — close your corpus gap
guide.s4d: Enter current age, retirement age, current savings, monthly investment and expected return. Read the projected corpus, then stress-test it: lower the return by 2 points and raise contributions until the corpus recovers.
guide.tip1: Run every important projection twice: a base case and a conservative case 2-3 points lower.
guide.tip2: Think in real terms: subtract ~2-3% inflation from nominal returns to judge purchasing power.
guide.tip3: Use Save State to bookmark scenarios in the URL, and Download PDF to keep a dated record.
guide.tip4: Switch currency in the header — the math is identical, only formatting changes.
guide.tip5: Revisit yearly: update balances and remaining years rather than starting from scratch.
guide.exportSave: Save State encodes your inputs into the page URL — bookmark it or send it to a partner or adviser to reproduce the exact scenario.
guide.exportPdf: Download PDF exports a dated summary (inputs, results, charts) for your records or annual reviews.
guide.exportLocal: All computation happens locally in your browser — your numbers are never uploaded. See the Privacy Policy for details.
